rationale: The book's entry survives comparison with the two strongest specific rivals. The traditional Protestant reading (works of the law = a fixed class of Mosaic deeds standing symbolically for legalism and self-reliant merit) and the New Perspective reading (works of the law = specifically Jewish boundary markers) each explain part of the supplied evidence and fail on the rest. The NPP reading cannot explain Galatians 3:10, where Paul defines the phrase's field by quoting Deuteronomy 27:26 — 'all things which are written in the book of the law' — a scope far wider than circumcision, food, and calendar; nor Romans 3:20, where the works are tied to the law's sin-identifying moral function. The traditional reading handles Romans 3 and Galatians 3:10 but strains against Galatians 2:11-16, where the phrase first appears amid a table-fellowship and circumcision-party dispute, and it tends to overflow into 'law abolished' or 'works themselves bad' conclusions that Romans 3:31 ('we establish the law'), Ephesians 2:9-10, and Romans 7:12-22 forbid. The book's core — that the phrase denotes context-identified deeds and uniformly denies the transactional claim made for them (that deeds purchase justification, the Spirit, or covenant standing) — explains all seven cited occurrences without forcing any of them: Romans 3:20, 28 and Galatians 3:10 as God's law, Galatians 2:16 as the circumcision-party application, Galatians 3:2, 5 as unnamed acts, with Romans 9:32's TR wording flagged honestly. Its Romans 4:4-5 wage/debt analysis supplies a concrete mechanism for the uniform denial (work as a claim on God as debtor, cf. Luke 17:10) that the rivals lack. No counter-reading accounts for a supplied text that the book's core cannot explain; the rivals' advantages are subsets of what the book already explains. PERSUADED with FULL scope, since the occurrence table and the End of the Law chapter support the entry's secondary claims (not a synonym for obedience; no single unchanging class) from the cited contexts themselves.
book_core_identification: 'Works of the law' (erga nomou) is not a code-word for one fixed class of deeds (neither legalism-in-general nor Jewish boundary markers specifically); the surrounding context identifies which deeds are in view (God's law in Rom 3:20, 28 and Gal 3:10; the circumcision-party's demand in Gal 2:16; unnamed acts in Gal 3:2, 5), and what Paul uniformly denies is the claim made for those deeds — that they can purchase justification, produce the Spirit, establish covenant standing, or place God in debt. The phrase attacks the deed's asserted purchase-power, not the deeds or the law as such.
book_secondary_elaborations: 'Works of the law' is not a synonym for obedience: a work is a deed, obedience names the deed's relation to a legitimate command, and the two meet in one act without merging (Luke 17:10; Heb 11:8; Jas 2:22).
Romans 4:4-5 defines the excluded work by its economic claim — work for wages makes God a debtor — supplying the mechanism of the uniform denial.
The textual note on Romans 9:32: the Received Text reads 'works of the law' while the critical text reads 'as it were by works,' shifting weight to the attempted manner rather than a hidden code.
Paul's named laws (law of God, law of sin, law of faith, law of Christ, commandments of men) show 'law' is not a single referent, so the phrase cannot be flattened into one bucket.
The 'not of works' family (Eph 2:9-10; Titus 3:5, 8; Rom 9:11; 2 Tim 1:9) excludes works as source and purchase price while restoring them as the life the gift creates.
Christ as telos of the law means purpose/destination, not termination (Rom 10:4 with Rom 3:31; 1 Tim 1:5-8; Rom 6:22).
strongest_counter_interpretation: The New Perspective on Paul (Sanders, Dunn, Wright): erga nomou is a fixed, specific referent — the Jewish covenant boundary markers of circumcision, food laws, and Sabbath/calendar observance that separated Jews from Gentiles. Paul's polemic targets ethnic exclusivism and the demand that Gentiles adopt Jewish identity badges, not human effort or merit-theology. Its evidential base: the phrase debuts in the Antioch table-fellowship dispute (Gal 2:11-16); circumcision is the letter's flashpoint (Gal 5:2-6; 6:12-15); Romans 3:28 is immediately followed by 'Is he the God of the Jews only?' (Rom 3:29-30); Acts 15 frames the controversy as circumcision for salvation; and 4QMMT provides a Second Temple parallel where 'works of the Torah' names sectarian halakhic rulings.
counter_core_identification: 'Works of the law' has one consistent referent throughout Paul: the badge-practices (circumcision, food laws, calendar observance) that marked Jewish covenant identity, so that Paul's denial targets ethnic boundary-drawing rather than a transactional claim about deeds purchasing standing before God.
material_core_denial: The NPP counter denies the book's core by asserting that the phrase does identify one unchanging class of deeds — the ethnic boundary markers — in every occurrence, and that Paul's target is exclusivism rather than the deed's claimed purchase-power; both cannot be true of the same phrase, since the book explicitly classifies Romans 3:20, 28 and Galatians 3:10 as God's law generally, not badges.
counter_case: Galatians 2:11-16: the phrase's first appearance grows directly out of Peter's withdrawal from Gentile table fellowship under pressure from 'them which were of the circumcision,' making Jew/Gentile separation the live issue.
Galatians 5:2-6 and 6:12-15: circumcision is the concrete demand throughout the letter, suggesting the disputed 'works' are identity markers.
Romans 3:29-30: Paul's very next move after 'justified by faith without the deeds of the law' is 'Is he the God of the Jews only?' — tying the denial to Jew/Gentile inclusion.
Acts 15:1: the historical controversy was framed as 'Except ye be circumcised... ye cannot be saved,' matching a boundary-marker referent.
4QMMT's 'some of the works of the Torah' shows the phrase circulating in Second Temple Judaism as a label for specific halakhic observances, not for moral effort in general.
book_explanatory_advantages: Galatians 3:10 quotes Deuteronomy 27:26 — 'all things which are written in the book of the law' — explicitly identifying the whole written Torah, which the book's context-driven classification accommodates and the boundary-marker reading cannot without shrinking 'all things' to three badges.
Romans 3:20 grounds the denial in 'by the law is the knowledge of sin' — the law's universal sin-identifying function ('no flesh'), which fits God's law generally, not ethnic markers.

The book explains the Jew/Gentile material the NPP relies on (Gal 2:12, 14 context words decide the Gal 2:16 classification; circumcision as demanded purchase price and covenant gate, per Gal 5:2-4 and Acts 15:1) without fixing that referent onto Romans 3.

Romans 4:4-5 plus Luke 17:10 supplies a mechanism — work as wage-claim making God a debtor — that unifies all occurrences under one denied claim, explaining why the same phrase can cover different deeds.

The book preserves Paul's own guard-rails that the traditional legalism-symbol reading strains against: 'we establish the law' (Rom 3:31), 'the law is holy... spiritual... I delight in the law of God' (Rom 7:12, 14, 22), and 'created... unto good works' (Eph 2:10).
The Romans 9:32 textual note (TR 'works of the law' vs. critical 'as it were by works') is handled transparently and actually strengthens the manner-of-seeking analysis over a fixed-referent code.
counter_explanatory_advantages: The NPP reading gives the most natural account of why the phrase debuts in a table-fellowship dispute (Gal 2:11-16) and why circumcision dominates Galatians.
It directly explains Romans 3:29-30's pivot to Jew/Gentile inclusion after 3:28.
It has an extrabiblical anchor (4QMMT) for the phrase as a known Second Temple expression for particular observances.
decisive_sources: Galatians 3:10 with Deuteronomy 27:26 ('the book of the law... all things written... to do them') — fixes at least one occurrence to God's whole law, defeating the fixed boundary-marker referent
Romans 3:20 ('by the law is the knowledge of sin... no flesh') with Romans 3:31 ('we establish the law') — the denial concerns justification-power, not the law's validity
Galatians 2:12, 14 — the context words that legitimately classify Gal 2:16 as a circumcision-party application
Romans 4:4-5 with Luke 17:10 — the wage/debt mechanism defining the excluded claim
Galatians 3:2, 5 — the Spirit-by-faith contrast with no disputed act named, showing the phrase's referent is context-supplied
Ephesians 2:9-10 and Titus 3:5, 8 — works excluded as purchase price, commanded as fruit
unresolved_objections: A defensible middle reading holds that erga nomou has a constant surface referent (deeds of the Mosaic Torah) applied in varied controversies, so the 'no unchanging class' claim may overstate the variation; Gal 2:16 arguably still means Torah-deeds even though the circumcision party is the occasion.
The Galatians 3:2, 5 classification as 'ambiguous/unnamed acts' is debatable, since the letter's live controversy (circumcision) plausibly names the act implicitly.
The Romans 9:32 entry depends on the KJV/TR reading; on the critical text that verse drops out of the phrase's occurrence list entirely.
The book does not engage 4QMMT, the strongest extrabiblical datum the sectarian-halakhah and NPP readings cite, so the phrase's Second Temple usage remains unaddressed.
